items.prompt: Order the initialization steps for computing each vertex's minimum unweighted distance to any vertex in a known source set S.

elements.text: Initialize every distance to infinity or unseen.
For every distinct source s in S, set distance[s] = 0 and mark it discovered.
Enqueue all distinct sources before processing any non-source vertex.
Run the ordinary BFS relaxation from the shared queue.

feedback.reason: All sources must occupy the same distance-zero frontier before expansion begins.

blocks.text: Build one complete distance-zero layer

items: Initialize every vertex distance to infinity or unseen.
For each distinct source s, set distance[s] = 0 and mark s discovered.
Enqueue every distinct source before removing any queue entry.
Run ordinary BFS, assigning each unseen neighbor distance[u] + 1.

blocks.text: The initial queue is one shared layer zero. Every later vertex is first claimed by the closest source wave. Running one source to completion before inserting the others would let source order, rather than minimum distance to the set, own early discoveries.

blocks.title: Initialization invariant
blocks.text: All distinct sources are discovered at distance zero and queued before expansion begins.

items.prompt: An unweighted road graph has 40 fire stations and millions of intersections. The task needs the distance from every intersection to its nearest station. Which approach matches the output contract?

options.text: Run a complete BFS from each station and take the minimum afterward.
Run BFS from one arbitrary station because BFS is always fastest.
Run one BFS seeded with all 40 stations at distance zero.
Run DFS from all stations; depth order automatically gives nearest distance.

feedback.reason: Simultaneous distance-zero sources let one breadth expansion compute the lower envelope of all source distances.

blocks.text: Forty origins compete in one breadth expansion

Seed all 40 stations at distance 0. Layer 1 contains intersections one road from at least one station, layer 2 contains the next unseen intersections, and so on. First discovery assigns each intersection the minimum edge count over all 40 possible origins.

items: One multi-source traversal with adjacency lists costs O(V + E).
Forty complete BFS runs cost O(40(V + E)) before taking per-vertex minima.
One arbitrary source omits the other 39 origins, while DFS does not finalize minimum unit-edge distance by first discovery.

blocks.title: Lower-envelope rule
blocks.text: Simultaneous equal-cost waves compute min over all source distances in one traversal.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.forty_bfs: This is correct but repeats graph traversal 40 times; simultaneous sources compute the same minimum-distance envelope in one traversal.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.one_arbitrary: One source computes distance to that station, not to the nearest station in the full set.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.dfs_nearest: DFS does not process unit-cost paths in nondecreasing length and cannot assign nearest distances by first discovery.

items.prompt: The supplied source list is [2, 2, 5]. What is the correct canonical initialization for multi-source BFS?

options.text: Enqueue vertex 2 twice so its wave has twice the priority of vertex 5.
Seed vertices 2 and 5 once each at distance zero and enqueue each once.
Set distance[2] = 2 because source 2 appears twice.
Leave both copies unseen until dequeue; late marking is always equivalent.

feedback.reason: The source set is semantic; duplicate input entries do not create distinct graph origins.

blocks.text: The source input denotes a set, not weighted priority

items: The distinct source identities in [2, 2, 5] are {2,5}.
Enqueue 2 once and 5 once; the repeated 2 contributes no new origin.

blocks.text: BFS priority comes from distance layers, not source multiplicity. Enqueuing 2 twice adds redundant work without improving any distance, and the number of appearances never changes a source's zero distance to itself. If two entries share a location but have different future-relevant state, such as different resource masks, they are distinct states rather than duplicates.

blocks.title: Deduplication rule
blocks.text: Deduplicate by the full search-state identity before seeding the distance-zero frontier.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.enqueue_duplicate: BFS priority is determined by distance layers, not multiplicity; duplicate sources add redundant frontier entries.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.distance_two: Source multiplicity does not change the zero distance from a source to itself.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.dequeue_mark: That intentionally admits duplicate scheduling and weakens the one-discovery invariant without changing the mathematical source set.

items.prompt: A contamination process starts simultaneously at several cells and spreads one orthogonal step per minute through open cells. What value gives the time until every open cell is contaminated, or reports that complete contamination is impossible?

options.text: The number of initial sources, because each source contributes one minute.
The largest queue size observed during BFS.
The maximum recursive DFS depth from any one source.
The maximum finite distance assigned by multi-source BFS, provided no required open cell remains unreachable.

feedback.reason: BFS distance is arrival time under unit-time moves, and completion occurs at the last reachable required state.

blocks.text: Arrival distance is contamination time

items: Seed every initially contaminated cell at distance 0.
Generate legal orthogonal moves through open cells; each BFS edge advances time by one minute.
Assign each newly reached cell its earliest arrival minute.
After BFS, fail if any open cell is unseen; otherwise return the largest assigned distance.

blocks.text: The maximum finite distance is when the last required cell becomes contaminated. Source count measures origins and maximum queue size measures frontier width; neither is elapsed time. DFS depth depends on exploration order rather than simultaneous earliest arrival.

blocks.title: Completion contract
blocks.text: Return max distance only after proving every required open cell has a finite distance.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.source_count: Source count changes how waves cover the grid but is not the propagation depth.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.queue_size: Queue width measures frontier memory pressure, not the number of elapsed propagation layers.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.dfs_depth: DFS depth depends on exploration order and does not represent simultaneous minimum arrival time.

items.prompt: Edges have nonnegative weights 1 or 7, and the task asks for the minimum cost to any of several sources. Is ordinary multi-source BFS sufficient?

options.text: Yes; multiple sources make BFS correct for arbitrary nonnegative weights.
Use multi-source DFS because depth-first traversal compares weighted routes more directly.
No; initialize all sources with distance zero in a multi-source Dijkstra priority queue.
Convert to an adjacency matrix; then FIFO BFS becomes weighted-correct.

feedback.reason: Multi-source initialization generalizes, but FIFO correctness still requires equal edge costs.

blocks.text: Multiple origins do not repair unequal edge costs

A one-edge route of cost 7 can enter a FIFO frontier before a two-edge route of total cost 1 + 1 = 2. Edge-count layers therefore do not order vertices by the requested accumulated cost, regardless of how many sources were seeded.

items: Set every source's tentative distance to 0 and insert all sources into a min-priority queue.
Remove the vertex with smallest tentative total cost.
Relax each outgoing edge and update the neighbor when the new accumulated cost is smaller.
Ignore stale priority entries or use an equivalent decrease-key discipline.

blocks.title: Frontier boundary
blocks.text: Use FIFO for equal edge costs, a 0–1 deque for weights 0 and 1, and Dijkstra's priority frontier for general nonnegative weights.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.ordinary_bfs: Multiple origins do not restore the equal-edge-cost invariant required by FIFO first discovery.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.dfs: DFS exploration order does not finalize the minimum accumulated weighted path cost.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.matrix: Changing the representation does not remove unequal edge weights from path costs.

items.prompt: Some connected component of an undirected graph contains no source. After a correct multi-source BFS from all sources, how should vertices in that component be represented?

options.text: The first unseen vertex should automatically become an additional source at distance zero.
They remain unseen or at infinite distance; the algorithm must not invent a nearest source across missing edges.
Assign them the largest distance found in another component.
An adjacency matrix implicitly connects the component to a source through zero entries.

feedback.reason: A source wave cannot cross a disconnected-component boundary.

blocks.text: No source means no finite path in that component

In an undirected graph, every path remains inside one connected component. A component containing no seeded source can never receive a queue entry from a source wave, so all of its vertices retain infinity or unseen.

blocks.title: Do not fabricate coverage
blocks.text: Promoting an unseen vertex to a new source changes the supplied source set. Copying another component's last distance invents a path, and a zero matrix cell represents an absent edge rather than a connection.

blocks.title: Unreachable-state rule
blocks.text: Multi-source BFS covers exactly the union of source-containing components.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.new_sources: That changes the supplied source set and turns the task into component coverage rather than nearest supplied source.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.last_distance: Distance requires a path; copying a numeric layer fabricates reachability.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.matrix_connect: Zero matrix entries normally mean absent edges, not zero-cost connections.

items.prompt: Which conceptual transformation explains why seeding all sources together computes distance to the nearest source in an unweighted graph?

options.text: Merge all source vertices into one physical vertex, even when they have different incident edges.
Duplicate every original edge once per source so each BFS wave has its own graph.
Build a DFS forest; every tree depth is automatically the nearest-source distance.
Add a virtual super-source with one edge to every real source, run BFS, and subtract that one virtual edge from reported distances.

feedback.reason: A virtual common origin places all real sources in the same first layer, equivalent to a shared distance-zero queue after offsetting the virtual edge.

blocks.text: A virtual origin proves the minimum-over-sources formula
Add a virtual vertex q with an outgoing unit edge q → s for every real source s. Any q-to-v path must first choose one such source, so `dist(q,v) = 1 + min_s dist(s,v)` for every reachable v.

Direct multi-source BFS removes q and the common +1 offset by placing every real source directly at distance 0. It does not physically merge their identities or neighborhoods, duplicate graph edges, or use DFS depth as distance.

blocks.title: Equivalence
blocks.text: A shared distance-zero queue is the offset-free implementation of BFS from a virtual super-source.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.merge_vertices: Merging changes the graph by combining source neighborhoods and can create paths that did not exist.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.duplicate_edges: That expands the graph unnecessarily and does not express the shared minimum-distance competition.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.dfs_forest: DFS depth is not minimum unweighted distance and depends on exploration order.
